extracted.intended_audience: speculative-fiction writers, fantasy/worldbuilding authors, and creative-writers interested in magic systems
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and criteria for designing and writing 'rule-less' or 'soft/numinous' magic in fiction — when to leave magic unexplained, how to handle internal consistency, and how that choice affects reader experience and story focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit rules when they aren't important to the story
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s okay to not have rules unless it is important to the story for the character or reader to understand them. The goal of the story can be that you don’t understand how the magic works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the mechanics do not affect what the story is about, resist explaining them. Example: King Arthur’s sword-in-the-stone — we don’t know how it works and we don’t need to. Anti-pattern: explaining mechanics simply because you can, which can pull focus from the story’s core.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose between hidden internal logic and apparent inconsistency
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two modes: (a) magic with internal logic that is never explained to the reader, and (b) magic that appears to have no internal logic and is inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use (a) when you want believable, consistent weirdness (the rules exist but are withheld). Use (b) when unpredictability and horror/dread are the point (e.g., the Monkey’s Paw). Be deliberate: each mode creates different reader expectations and narrative consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create wonder or dread as intended reader effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule-less magic can produce a sense of wonder and awe, or a sense of dread and fear depending on tone and consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which emotional response you want (wonder vs. dread). Examples: numinous magic often evokes awe; eldritch/terrifying magic (lazy gun, monkey’s paw) creates dread. Use the magic’s opacity to scale those feelings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve infodump equity — allocate page weight carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Save pages and explanations; infodump equity means readers give you permission to explain things when they’re genuinely curious, so spend that equity where it matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnecessary worldbuilding dumps. If readers are curious about one element, that is the place to spend exposition; avoid dumping on unrelated mechanics that divert attention and bore readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only explain magic that affects character wants or goal-achievement
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless information affects why we care about something or how a character will achieve their goal, the reader doesn’t actually need to know the mechanics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: does this detail change our understanding of the character’s motivations or means? If not, omit. Example: you don’t need to explain how a spaceship works unless it influences plot or desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let characters search for patterns and be wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: People and characters will try to find patterns or rules; showing their (mis)applied theories can enrich the world and underscore the magic’s unknowability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make attempts at pattern-finding part of characterization and plot: they can be plausible-but-false rules characters cling to. This creates realism and can produce irony or tragedy when those patterns fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide at least one consistent anchor or 'thing to hang onto'
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in rule-less systems, often there is one small consistent element characters believe in or that you keep consistent for believability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: not repeating a phrase three times, a bus arriving when you walk away, or a single cultural superstition. That single consistency helps readers accept broader inconsistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use magic as a MacGuffin or narrative driver rather than a technical focus
rubrics_metrics.description: If the mystery of the magical object/force drives desire or conflict, let that wanting propel the story instead of technical mechanics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the lazy gun or Bookburners’ rising tide — the unknown power motivates characters. Make the mystery the plot engine; avoid turning it into a how-it-works puzzle unless that’s the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invent internal rules invisibly for verisimilitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors can (and often should) generate rules, languages, or numerology behind the scenes so that on-the-page behavior feels consistent even when the rules aren’t revealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may create detailed back-end logic you never explain; doing so helps you write consistently (e.g., constructed language lines, numerology that informs two lines of dialogue). This is different from dumping those rules on the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid detailed technical explanations (handwavium leads to more questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Committing to detailed scientific/technical mechanisms invites further questions and can unravel your intended story focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If explaining physics or mechanics will open a cascade of new questions, opt to handwave or withhold. Anti-pattern: giving a math/physics infodump that derails tone and pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use unpredictability of consequences to explore theme
rubrics_metrics.description: When characters can't know the consequences of using magic (Monkey’s Paw model), the story can explore the human cost of engaging with incomprehensible forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the stakes about the consequences and character choices rather than mastery. Showing attempts to control or limit the magic can itself be thematic fodder (e.g., the more you try to constrain it, the worse it becomes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prime the pump — place exposition where curiosity is raised
rubrics_metrics.description: Place necessary exposition where it answers the questions you intentionally provoke; prime readers properly before explaining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want to explain something later, seed curiosity and cues earlier so the explanation lands. Misplaced infodumps (explaining the wrong thing at the wrong time) bore readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: In collaborative/serial work, evolve guidelines over time
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple authors or seasons are involved, you may start by trying weird things and later develop internal guidelines to maintain a coherent arc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Bookburners — early episodes experimented; later seasons codified ‘what is actually going on’ to support the series arc. Useful approach: discovery writing followed by establishing consistent behind-the-scenes rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of reader vs. character knowledge and its narrative effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the reader, the characters, or both will know any given piece of magic-related information — the difference changes suspense and perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: hobbits experience Gandalf as mysterious (reader aligned with them) while appendix material can give external readers more info. Align knowledge intentionally to control tension and wonder.
